title: The year in one sitting
hook: the poem, the disciples, the songs, the tales, the roads, the teachers, the history
tomorrow: Year three close: the great story

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chotrul Duchen, the day of miracles: Pindola's bowl ground to powder, the twin miracle, and a verse that says do the good thing again. Your line: good deeds multiply. Did you do it twice? Day one thousand sixty.

Near the top of a long climb, a hiker stops, turns around, and looks back down the trail. From up there the switchbacks that felt endless are just a few lines on a hillside, and the whole path makes sense at once. Tomorrow this year closes. So today, before the last step, turn around. One sitting, one look back over a year that began with a poem and ended with festivals.
screen: `STOP NEAR THE TOP.` → `TURN AROUND.` → `ONE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: It began with a poem. Ashvaghosha's Buddhacarita told the life as an epic: the palace, the king's fear, and the old man the gods placed on the prince's road so that he would see. Then came the disciples. Sariputta and Moggallana, the friends who went looking together. Ananda, who remembered. Mahakassapa in his rag robe. The women who asked to be ordained, and the whole sangha, wise and proud and forgetful, all welcome. Then the songs of the elders, in their own words: Patacara watching a lamp's wick drawn down until the flame went out, and Mutta, free of the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband. Then the long tales of the Jataka: Sumedha lying down in the mud so a Buddha of the past could walk across him, and the caravan leader who kept the water when spirits told him to throw it away. Then the roads. Councils where the elders recited the teaching from memory. Monks traveling with merchants along the Silk Road, translators like Kumarajiva, and Faxian setting out on foot for India. Then the teachers: Nagarjuna's middle way, Asanga tending a wounded dog, Shantideva, thought lazy, standing up to recite a long poem on the bodhisattva's way. Then history, held honestly: monasteries closed and reopened, Cambodia's sangha rebuilt from few, the empty niches at Bamiyan. And these last days, the festival year: a lamp at Vesak, sweet tea for the baby Buddha, a circle dance, a robe, a week of sitting, a day of miracles. Look at it from up here. The switchbacks were a poem, a song, a tale, a road, a teacher, a hard chapter. From this height they are one trail, and you walked all of it.
screen: `A POEM, THEN THE DISCIPLES.` · `SONGS AND LONG TALES.` · `ROADS, TEACHERS, HISTORY.` · then, large: `ONE TRAIL, SEEN FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. The bell will hold two minutes now. The path suggests twenty, so if you have them later today, give the year twenty minutes. For now, sit, and let one picture from this year come back by itself. Don't choose it. Whatever arrives first: a lamp, a bowl, a road, a dog, a robe, a face. Stay with it. Notice what your mind kept when you weren't trying to keep anything. The bell holds the time.
Buddhacarita. The poem that opened this year, now seen whole with the disciples, the songs, the tales, the roads, the teachers, the history, the festivals. Today's word.
Your line: look how far. Today, tell someone one story from this year, the one that stayed with you, in two sentences. Day one thousand sixty.

screen: `DAY 1060 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR THREE CLOSE: THE GREAT STORY.`

howItsDone: Some Buddhist communities mark the end of a period of study or a retreat with a longer sitting and a review of what was learned, sometimes followed by a dedication of merit.

fork.setup: you're a caravan leader crossing a desert. spirits on the road tell you there's water ahead, so throw away what you carry. what do you do?
options: throw it away and travel light
send scouts and throw away half
fork.reveal: the leader in the Jataka keeps the water and his caravan comes through. it was one of this year's tales.

original.note: Sanskrit Buddhacarita: Ashvaghosha's poem of the Buddha's life, where this year began.

trapdoor: what you thought: a year of separate lessons.
what it means: one story, from a poem about a prince to festivals people keep today.

what a scholar hears: an epic, the songs of the first nuns and monks, the birth tales, the chronicles of councils and roads, and the teachers' lives, each a different kind of text, all carrying one story.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga XI (the first council); Legge, Fa-hien (1886)

notes: A summary of year three's blocks (days 697–1059); every item is taken from the year-three outline and the scripts written to it. Check that each detail matches how its own day was finally told (e.g. Mahakassapa's rag robe, Sariputta and Moggallana 'looking together', Mutta's three crooked things, Asanga's dog as legend).
The Asanga story is a legend; it is named here only in passing.
No counts of days, tales or years spoken on purpose.
The hook uses a hikers' image rather than a tradition claim.
The fork reuses Jataka 1 (two caravans) as a review item; confirm the Jataka telling (the leader who kept water).
Editor pass: the hook no longer claims hikers in general 'have a habit'; Shantideva's 'masterpiece' (an unsourced superlative) became 'a long poem on the bodhisattva's way'.
Audit pass: the teach's closing line ('one story, carried by many people, each handing it to the next') duplicated day 1061's hand-to-hand image the next day; 1060 now closes on its own hiking image.
